clue.text: Writer editing papers

indicators.note: editing reworks a text, so the letters of papers are rearranged

explanation.surface: An author busily editing a stack of papers.
explanation.walkthrough: SAPPER was the pen name of H. C. McNeile, author of the Bulldog Drummond stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapper is the pseudonym of a popular British thriller novelist.

clue.text: What makes one maty ?

indicators.note: makes is read as forms or rearranges into, so the letters are reshaped

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A question asking what turns someone friendly.
explanation.walkthrough: I (one) plus MATY, rearranged as 'makes' signals, gives the answer, and friendship is exactly what makes a person matey.
explanation.definitionFit: Friendliness between people is what makes them pals, so goodwill fits.

clue.text: It's irrelevant to be more polite, indicating direction

definitions.text: to be more polite, indicating direction
definitions.meaning: pointing at people is rude, so politeness means doing less of it when showing the way

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer into POINT LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without purpose is futile; and showing the way politely means jabbing a finger less.

clue.text: Trot, badly at point-to point hence this equestrian row?

indicators.note: badly signals the letters of trot are put into a poor, jumbled order

parts.note: two compass points, E for east and N for north

explanation.surface: A horse trotting poorly at a point-to-point race meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotten Row is the track for horse riding in London's Hyde Park; a point-to-point is a British amateur steeplechase.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotten Row is the famous riding track in Hyde Park, so the word completes its name.

clue.text: No point introducing a Pole as Animal Farm boss

indicators.note: introducing means bringing something into the middle of another piece

parts.note: taken as written
a Pole, a person from Poland, taken as written
N, the compass point north

explanation.surface: Bringing a Polish man in as leader of Orwell's farm, without good reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Introducing' has the Pole and article brought in after the first letter; Animal Farm is Orwell's allegory, its boss pig named after the French emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: In Orwell's fable the pig called after the French emperor becomes the tyrant who runs the farm.

clue.text: Book makes cardinal point with rage to church

parts.note: north is one of the four cardinal compass points
rage means anger
an abbey is a church of a monastery

explanation.surface: A furious journey towards a church at a compass bearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's novel set partly in Bath is a classic of English literature.

clue.text: Rip gets tiddly — 'e's under influence

indicators.note: tiddly means slightly drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: 'e is the dropped-aitch he, giving the letter E

explanation.surface: A drunken man called Rip, slurring that he is under the influence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tiddly' is British slang for tipsy; it scrambles RIPGETS with E.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing or prestige gives a person sway over others, so it is a kind of influence.

clue.text: The drink in France makes more halt

definitions.meaning: the drink is slang for the sea
halt means lame, so more halt is more lame

explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' is slang for the sea; 'halt' is an old word for limping.
explanation.definitionFit: In French the sea is la mer; and limping worse makes one more crippled.

clue.text: Sailoring turned out badly for such as Alexander Selkirk

indicators.note: something that turned out badly went wrong, so the letters go awry

explanation.surface: A seafaring life that ended in misfortune for a marooned Scottish sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: Selkirk, marooned on a Pacific island, was the real-life model for Robinson Crusoe, so he and his like are the models behind fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Selkirk was the real person a famous fictional castaway was based on, a model or prototype.

clue.text: Land's End (European version)

parts.note: Land's End is the westernmost tip of Cornwall; the Spanish cape whose Latin-derived name means end of the earth is its continental counterpart

explanation.definitionFit: The Galician cape's name comes from Latin for the end of the earth, matching the Cornish headland's name.

clue.text: She's game, if old

parts.note: add old before this woman and you have the name of a card game

explanation.walkthrough: Old Maid is a children's card game; 'game' also suggests a willing woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A young female servant or girl; prefixed by old she names a card game.

clue.text: Consumers' viewpoints ?

parts.note: consumers are things that eat, and viewpoints read as points below the eyes: the pointed canines

explanation.definitionFit: Canine teeth sit beneath the eyes and are sharp points used in eating.

clue.text: Yorked by fast delivery, Dick

parts.note: a cricket picture of a batsman bowled by a fast ball, really the legendary highwayman's swift ride to York

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman is yorked by a ball pitching at his feet; Dick Turpin, the highwayman, was said to have ridden overnight to York.
explanation.definitionFit: The 18th-century highwayman Dick is linked by legend to a famous dash to York.

clue.text: Cheese needs end cut off, in short

indicators.note: losing its end means the final letter of the word is removed

parts.note: in short means brief

explanation.surface: A recipe says the cheese needs trimming, briefly put.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft French cheese.

clue.text: Judge cut short and in difficulty — hence majority verdicts

indicators.note: cut short means the final letter is removed

parts.note: a referee is a judge in a contest

indicators.note: in difficulty means in trouble, so the letters of and are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A judge truncated, in trouble, and so majority verdicts follow.
explanation.walkthrough: REFERE (referee less its last E) plus NDA (a jumble of AND).
explanation.definitionFit: Public votes on a single question are decided by the majority, so they are majority verdicts.

clue.text: Flier gets shock in the dark

parts.note: the dark means night
a jar is a jolt or shock

explanation.surface: A pilot gets a fright flying in darkness.
explanation.definitionFit: The nightjar is a nocturnal bird, so it flies.

clue.text: Man-eater, perhaps girl found in bed

parts.note: a tiger is a well-known man-eater
Lily is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A predatory girl discovered in a bed.
explanation.definitionFit: This orange lily is a garden flower grown in a flower bed.

clue.text: Reds — number turning up in trading-places

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: marts are places for trading

indicators.note: in a down entry turning up means the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: six is a number

explanation.surface: Communists appearing in markets in growing numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'turning up' reads the number from the bottom; 'trading-places' are markets.
explanation.definitionFit: Communists, followers of Karl Marx, are colloquially called Reds.

clue.text: No longer coaching or playing

parts.note: off the stagecoach, and not on the theatre stage acting

explanation.definitionFit: Out of the coach and out of view of the audience, both readings of off the stage.

clue.text: Extract from magistrate's concise summing-up

indicators.note: an extract is a piece taken out of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A summary taken from a magistrate's brief closing remarks.
explanation.definitionFit: The essence or main point of something is a brief summary of it.

clue.text: Way to bend a stiffener

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
to arch is to bend

explanation.surface: A method for bending something rigid.
explanation.definitionFit: Laundry starch is used to stiffen fabric.

clue.text: For Labour leader one vote short? On the contrary

parts.note: pro means for, in favour

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
X is the cross marked on a ballot

explanation.surface: A Labour leader falling one vote short of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' flips 'short' into its opposite, long-winded.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordy speech is the opposite of brief.

clue.text: Young lady-love appears somewhat ropy

parts.note: a lass is a young lady
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A girlfriend's looks seem a bit poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ropy' is British slang for poor quality; here it means made of rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy's noose is made of rope, so it is rather rope-like.

clue.text: Object in space provided, as editor ordered

indicators.note: ordered means put in order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An item given space in a publication, as the editor instructed.
explanation.definitionFit: A minor planet is a rocky body orbiting the Sun.

clue.text: Female one, connects with Descartes

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
René is the first name of the French philosopher

explanation.surface: A woman makes contact with the French philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's name, so a female.

clue.text: Odd parts of innings for Taverners to enjoy

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters, first, third, fifth and seventh

explanation.surface: Cricket teams sharing innings for a club called the Taverners.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lord's Taverners are a British charity cricket side, but here taverners are innkeepers or drinkers.
explanation.definitionFit: Pubs are where tavern-goers drink and enjoy themselves.

clue.text: Serious types making up Temperance League?

definitions.text: Serious types making up Temperance League?

parts.words: Serious types making up Temperance League?
parts.note: grave people, pictured as the teams that would play in a league of teetotallers

explanation.definitionFit: Earnest, humourless people, read as teams of the abstinent.

clue.text: In blaze of publicity? Very well

definitions.meaning: in a celebrated way, widely known
excellently, as in getting on like a house on fire

explanation.definitionFit: Being renowned means acting in the public eye; colloquially the adverb also means splendidly.

clue.text: Tomboy follows duck in park with pole

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: Hyde Park in London
a duck is a zero score in cricket, the letter O
N is the north pole

explanation.surface: A boisterous girl chasing ducks in a London park beside a pole.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyde Park is a large park in central London.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowdy, boisterous girl is a tomboy.
